regions.name: Umbria
regions.summary: Umbria is the green heart of Italy, the one region with neither a coastline nor a foreign border, hill country between Tuscany and the Adriatic side of the Apennines. Two wines carry its name on an exam: Montefalco Sagrantino, a DOCG made entirely from the most tannic grape in Italy, dry or as a sweet passito; and Orvieto, a white of Grechetto and Trebbiano from a volcanic plateau on the Lazio border. Torgiano Rosso Riserva, a Sangiovese led DOCG built by one family near Perugia, is the third. Sangiovese fills most of the red vineyard; Grechetto and Trebbiano Spoletino are the whites to know.

terroir.climate: Continental with a Mediterranean summer: hot, dry days from June to September, cold winters and real spring frost risk in the valleys. The Apennines to the east shut out the Adriatic, so Umbria is more continental and more sharply seasonal than coastal Tuscany; Lake Trasimeno softens its own shore. Montefalco's long autumn lets Sagrantino hang into October to ripen its tannin.
terroir.soils: Clay and limestone on the Montefalco ridge, with sandy marine deposits and pebbles on its slopes. Orvieto sits on a cliff of volcanic tuff, the ash of the Vulsini volcanoes, with clay and sand beneath it. Torgiano works alluvial clay and sand where the Chiascio meets the Tiber. Lake Trasimeno's shore is light clay and sand over limestone.
terroir.topography: A land of hills and small basins: the Tiber valley runs the length of it, the Valle Umbra opens below Assisi, Spoleto and Montefalco, and the Apennine ridge walls the east. Montefalco's vineyards climb the slopes below a hill town of about 470 metres that looks over the whole plain. Orvieto's zone is a tuff plateau cut by the Paglia valley.
terroir.water: The Tiber is the spine, fed by the Chiascio at Torgiano and the Paglia at Orvieto; the Corbara reservoir on the Tiber gives Lago di Corbara DOC its name. Lake Trasimeno, the largest lake of peninsular Italy, moderates the vineyards of the Colli del Trasimeno DOC on its shores.

grapes.name: Sagrantino
grapes.styles: Montefalco's own grape, thick skinned and small bunched, with the highest tannin and polyphenol load measured in any Italian variety: dry wines of blackberry, dried plum and black tea that need years, and a sweet passito from dried bunches.

grapes.name: Sangiovese
grapes.styles: The workhorse red of the region: the base of Montefalco Rosso, of Torgiano Rosso Riserva and of most of the IGT reds, lighter and more rustic than in Tuscany.

grapes.name: Grechetto
grapes.styles: The white of Orvieto and Colli Martani: thick skinned, resistant to rot, nutty and faintly bitter with pear and white flowers, and the better half of the Orvieto blend. Grechetto di Todi is a separate variety, Pignoletto by another name.

grapes.name: Trebbiano Toscano
grapes.styles: Procanico in Orvieto, where it stretches the Grechetto with neutral, crisp volume; most of the Orvieto blend by history, less of it by choice today.

grapes.name: Trebbiano Spoletino
grapes.styles: A distinct Trebbiano from Spoleto and Montefalco, late ripening and high in acid, often grown up trees in the old way; it gives citrus, herb and salt, sometimes skin fermented.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.styles: Permitted in Montefalco Rosso and widely planted for the IGT reds, where it softens Sagrantino and Sangiovese.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: A partner in the Umbria IGT reds and in Torgiano's broader DOC; never in Sagrantino.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Grown around Orvieto for barrel fermented whites sold as Umbria IGT, the most famous of them blended with Grechetto.

wines.note: Opaque, black fruited and fiercely tannic, with dried plum, cocoa and black tea; it is held in wood and bottle for over three years before sale and still wants a decade. Decant and serve with roast lamb, wild boar or aged pecorino.
The original form: bunches dried for weeks, then fermented into a sweet, tannic red of fig and blackberry. The local match is the Easter lamb or a dark chocolate cake, poured in a small glass.
Sangiovese led with a measured share of Sagrantino for grip: cherry, dried herbs and firm tannin, ready years before the Sagrantino is. The everyday red of the zone, with pasta and grilled sausages.

Grechetto and Trebbiano, dry and light to medium in weight, with pear, almond and a bitter twist; Classico from the hills around the town, Superiore with more ripeness. Lake fish, fritto misto and the region's black truffle dishes.

A botrytised Orvieto from the foggy valleys by the Paglia and Lake Corbara, golden and honeyed with apricot and saffron; the abboccato and amabile styles are its lighter, older cousins. Serve with blue cheese or fruit tarts.
Sangiovese led, aged at least three years and built to last: sour cherry, leather and tobacco with a firm, dry finish. Pigeon, game birds and braised beef.
Bright and saline, lemon peel and bitter herbs, sometimes amber from time on the skins; a newer white sold under the Spoleto DOC or as IGT. Grilled fish, strangozzi with truffle, fresh cheeses.

made.viticulture: Montefalco's vineyards sit on the ridge and the slopes below the town, mostly spur pruned cordon and Guyot at moderate density, with the old vine training up maple and elm trees surviving in a few Trebbiano Spoletino plots. Sagrantino is a thick skinned grape that resists rot but ripens late; growers leave it into October for the tannin to soften on the vine, and it is picked by hand, with the passito bunches chosen for their looseness so that they dry without mould. Sangiovese and the whites come in weeks earlier. Orvieto's plateau grows Grechetto and Procanico on tuff that drains fast, and the autumn fog in the Paglia valley is what the muffa nobile producers count on. Torgiano's low hills by the Tiber are warm enough to ripen Sangiovese fully. The hazards are spring frost in the basins, hail in summer and, for Sagrantino, a wet October that spoils the drying. Lake Trasimeno's shore gives a gentler climate for the region's Gamay, which is in fact Grenache under a local name.
made.winemaking: Dry Sagrantino is a wine of the 1970s; before that the grape was dried and made sweet for the church calendar. The dry wine is fermented with long maceration, two to four weeks, to extract and begin to polymerise the tannin, then aged in a mix of large casks and barrique for well over a year and held in bottle, because the rules ask thirty-seven months in all before release with at least twelve in wood and four in bottle. The passito is fermented slowly from bunches dried on racks for weeks, often into the winter, and keeps both sugar and a wall of tannin. Montefalco Rosso is made like a Tuscan Sangiovese, with the Sagrantino share giving colour and grip. Orvieto is cool fermented in steel to keep it light, Grechetto often with a short skin contact for texture; the sweet versions are either arrested to leave sugar (abboccato, amabile, dolce) or made from botrytised bunches picked late. Torgiano Rosso Riserva takes three years of ageing before release. Umbria IGT lets the cellar blend Chardonnay with Grechetto in barrel or make Bordeaux style reds.

law.classification: Umbria holds two DOCGs. Torgiano Rosso Riserva was raised in 1990 from the Torgiano DOC of 1968, a Sangiovese led red with three years of ageing; Montefalco Sagrantino followed in 1992 from its 1979 DOC and must be Sagrantino alone, dry (secco) or passito. Around them sit the DOCs: Montefalco for the Sangiovese led Rosso and the Bianco, Orvieto (1971, shared with Lazio) with its Classico heart and Superiore tier, Torgiano for the wider family of wines, Colli Martani for Grechetto, Spoleto for Trebbiano Spoletino, Lago di Corbara and Rosso Orvietano beside Orvieto, Colli del Trasimeno, Colli Perugini, Colli Altotiberini, Amelia (once Colli Amerini), Assisi and Todi. Umbria IGT covers the region, and the cellars use it for Chardonnay, Grechetto blends and Bordeaux grape reds.
tiers: Montefalco Sagrantino DOCG
100 per cent Sagrantino; the dry wine ages 37 months with at least 12 in wood and 4 in bottle; the Passito, from dried grapes, shares the DOCG. DOC 1979, DOCG 1992.
Torgiano Rosso Riserva DOCG
Sangiovese led; at least three years of ageing before release; DOC Torgiano 1968, Riserva raised to DOCG in 1990.
Montefalco DOC
Rosso: Sangiovese led with at least 10 per cent Sagrantino, 18 months of ageing, Riserva 30; Bianco a white of Grechetto and Trebbiano.
Orvieto DOC

Grechetto and Procanico (Trebbiano Toscano) at least 60 per cent together; Classico from the hills around the town; Superiore with higher alcohol and lower yields; secco, abboccato, amabile, dolce and the botrytised muffa nobile.
Colli Martani DOC
The Grechetto DOC of the Martani hills south of Perugia; Todi holds a DOC of its own for the Grechetto di Todi vine.
Spoleto DOC
A DOC of 2011 for Trebbiano Spoletino as a still, sparkling or passito white.
Umbria IGT
The regional catch all, where the barrel fermented Chardonnay and Grechetto whites and the Bordeaux blend reds are sold.
labels: Passito
wine from dried grapes; Montefalco Sagrantino Passito is the sweet original of the zone
Secco
dry; printed on Montefalco Sagrantino to separate it from the Passito
Classico
the Orvieto hills around the town itself, the historic heart of the DOC
Superiore

Muffa Nobile

places.name: Montefalco
places.note: A hill town between Foligno and Spoleto called the balcony of Umbria, whose ridge and four neighbouring communes (Bevagna, Gualdo Cattaneo, Castel Ritaldi and Giano dell'Umbria) grow Sagrantino on clay, limestone and sandy marine deposits. The DOCG covers the dry wine and the passito; the DOC Rosso and Bianco share the same hills.

places.name: Bevagna
places.note: The commune on the plain below Montefalco, inside the DOCG, with lower sites at the edge of the plain.

places.name: Orvieto
places.note: A cathedral town on a tuff cliff above the Paglia, the DOC named for it stretching east along the Tiber and south into Lazio. Classico covers the hills closest to the town; the lower Paglia valley gives the fog for the muffa nobile wines. Antinori's Castello della Sala estate lies inside the zone and sells its Chardonnay and Grechetto whites as Umbria IGT.

places.name: Lago di Corbara
places.note: A DOC of 1998 on the reservoir of the Tiber beside Orvieto, for reds from Sangiovese, Cabernet, Merlot and Pinot Nero.

places.name: Torgiano
places.note: A village at the meeting of the Chiascio and the Tiber south of Perugia, whose DOC of 1968 was one of Italy's early ones and whose Rosso Riserva became a DOCG in 1990; the zone was built almost alone by the Lungarotti house, whose Rubesco Riserva Vigna Monticchio is the reference wine.

places.name: Colli Martani and Todi
places.note: The hills south of Perugia around Todi and Giano dell'Umbria, the DOC home of Grechetto as a varietal white; Grechetto di Todi is a different vine from Grechetto di Orvieto.

places.name: Spoleto
places.note: The Spoleto DOC of 2011 covers the old Trebbiano Spoletino vineyards south of Montefalco, a late ripening white once trained up trees and now the region's most talked about new wine.

places.name: Colli del Trasimeno
places.note: The DOC on the shores of Lake Trasimeno, west of Perugia, for Sangiovese reds, Grechetto whites and the local Gamay del Trasimeno, which is Grenache.

places.name: Lazio, the neighbour to the south
places.note: The sheet carries no Lazio locator, so its wines sit here: Frascati from the volcanic Castelli Romani hills south of Rome (Malvasia and Trebbiano, Frascati Superiore and Cannellino di Frascati at DOCG since 2011), Est! Est!! Est!!! di Montefiascone on Lake Bolsena, Cesanese del Piglio DOCG for the region's native red, and the Lazio side of the Orvieto DOC.

producers.name: Arnaldo Caprai
producers.why: The estate that made dry Sagrantino a modern wine through clonal research with the University of Milan from the late 1980s; its 25 Anni bottling is the zone's best known label.

producers.name: Paolo Bea
producers.why: A small Montefalco family estate working without additions, long macerations and late release: the natural wine reference for Sagrantino and Montefalco Rosso.

producers.name: Lungarotti
producers.why: The house that built Torgiano from the 1960s, won it a DOC in 1968 and its Rosso Riserva a DOCG in 1990; Rubesco Riserva Vigna Monticchio is the wine.

producers.name: Castello della Sala
producers.why: Antinori's Orvieto estate, whose barrel fermented Cervaro della Sala (Chardonnay with Grechetto) and botrytised Muffato della Sala showed what Umbria IGT could be.

producers.name: Adanti
producers.why: One of the early estates of dry Sagrantino, at Arquata near Bevagna, known for classic, slow Montefalco.

producers.name: Antonelli San Marco
producers.why: A Montefalco estate of 1881 known for restrained, organic Sagrantino and a serious Trebbiano Spoletino.

producers.name: Tabarrini
producers.why: Single vineyard Sagrantino from Montefalco's Turrita side and a textured Trebbiano Spoletino; a grower's estate of the new generation.

producers.name: Decugnano dei Barbi
producers.why: An Orvieto Classico estate on the Corbara side that revived botrytised Orvieto and makes a metodo classico sparkling from the same hills.

producers.name: Barberani
producers.why: Organic Orvieto Classico Superiore from the Corbara shore, with the Calcaia muffa nobile as its sweet flagship.

exam: Montefalco Sagrantino: 100 per cent Sagrantino, DOCG since 1992, 37 months of ageing with 12 in wood, dry or passito; the most tannic grape in Italy.
Orvieto: Grechetto and Trebbiano (Procanico), DOC 1971, shared with Lazio, Classico and Superiore, sweet versions from abboccato to muffa nobile.
Torgiano Rosso Riserva: Sangiovese led DOCG of 1990, three years of ageing, the Lungarotti zone; Torgiano DOC dates from 1968.
Montefalco Rosso is Sangiovese led with a compulsory Sagrantino share; do not call it a lesser Sagrantino.
Umbria's geography: landlocked, no foreign border, Tiber, Lake Trasimeno, Apennines to the east, Tuscany to the west.
The whites by name: Grechetto (Orvieto, Colli Martani), Trebbiano Spoletino (Spoleto), Chardonnay and Grechetto blends as Umbria IGT.
Castello della Sala and its two famous IGT whites are an Umbrian answer, not a Tuscan one, though the Antinori family of Florence has owned the estate since 1940.
traps: Sagrantino di Montefalco and Montefalco Sagrantino name the same DOCG; the second is the form the rules use today.
Montefalco Rosso is a Sangiovese blend; Montefalco Sagrantino is pure Sagrantino. The DOC and the DOCG share a town, not a grape rule.
Orvieto is a white wine zone; Rosso Orvietano and Lago di Corbara are the separate red DOCs beside it.
Grechetto di Orvieto and Grechetto di Todi are two different vines; the Todi one is Emilia's Pignoletto.
Gamay del Trasimeno is Grenache, not the Beaujolais grape.
The Orvieto DOC crosses into Lazio; Umbria shares it rather than owning it outright.
Trebbiano Spoletino is a separate variety, not Trebbiano Toscano grown near Spoleto.

cards.b: The dry wine: 37 months in all before release, at least 12 in wood and 4 in bottle. It is 100 per cent Sagrantino, DOC 1979 and DOCG 1992.
Montefalco Sagrantino (1992) and Torgiano Rosso Riserva (1990). Both red; Orvieto, the famous white, is a DOC.

cards.f: Orvieto: which grapes, and in what share?
cards.b: Grechetto and Procanico, the local name for Trebbiano Toscano, at least 60 per cent together, with other permitted whites for the rest. Grechetto gives the nut and bitter twist, Procanico the crisp volume.

cards.f: Torgiano Rosso Riserva: what it is
cards.b: A Sangiovese led DOCG (1990) near Perugia with at least three years of ageing, built by Lungarotti; Rubesco Riserva Vigna Monticchio is the reference bottle.

cards.f: How does Montefalco Rosso differ from Montefalco Sagrantino?
cards.b: Rosso: DOC, Sangiovese led with a compulsory Sagrantino share, 18 months of ageing. Sagrantino: DOCG, pure Sagrantino, 37 months.

cards.f: Why is Sagrantino famous among grapes?
cards.b: It carries the highest tannin and polyphenol content measured in an Italian variety; thick skins, small bunches, late ripening, and a history as a sweet passito for the church.
A distinct Trebbiano from Spoleto and Montefalco, late ripening and high in acid, once trained up trees; Spoleto DOC since 2011, citrus and salt, sometimes skin fermented.
Landlocked central Italy with no foreign border; Tuscany to the west, the Apennines and Marche to the east, Lazio to the south. The Tiber runs through it; Lake Trasimeno lies in the west.

questions.q: Which grape leads the blend of Montefalco Rosso?
questions.exp: Montefalco Rosso is Sangiovese led with a compulsory Sagrantino share of at least 10 per cent; Sagrantino alone makes the DOCG. Merlot is a permitted minor partner and Montepulciano is Abruzzo's grape.

questions.q: What is the minimum total ageing for Montefalco Sagrantino before release?
questions.exp: The rules ask 37 months in all, with at least 12 in wood and 4 in bottle. Eighteen months is Montefalco Rosso, 30 its Riserva, and 24 is Chianti Classico Riserva.

questions.q: Which two grapes make up the required majority of an Orvieto blend?
questions.exp: Orvieto must be at least 60 per cent Grechetto and Procanico together, Procanico being the local name for Trebbiano Toscano; other local whites fill the rest.

questions.q: Umbria's Sangiovese led Rosso Riserva DOCG is named for which town near Perugia?
questions.exp: Torgiano Rosso Riserva, a DOCG since 1990, is Sangiovese led and aged at least three years. Montefalco and Bevagna lie in the Sagrantino DOCG, and Todi is a Grechetto town with a DOC of its own.

questions.q: Which term on an Orvieto label marks a sweet wine made from botrytised grapes?
questions.exp: Muffa nobile, noble rot, names the botrytised Orvieto from the foggy valleys of the Paglia and Lake Corbara. Abboccato and amabile are the lighter off dry and medium sweet grades; Classico names the hills around the town.

questions.q: Which region shares the Orvieto DOC with Umbria?
questions.exp: The Orvieto zone runs south from the town across the border into the province of Viterbo in Lazio, so the DOC belongs to both regions.

questions.q: Besides the dry secco, in which style may Montefalco Sagrantino be made?
questions.exp: The DOCG also covers the passito, a sweet, tannic red from bunches dried for weeks. It is the older form, made for the church calendar before dry Sagrantino arrived in the 1970s.

regions.name: Abruzzo
regions.summary: Abruzzo is the mountainous region east of Rome whose vineyards run down from the Apennines to the Adriatic. One grape rules it: Montepulciano, dark, soft and generous, the grape and not the Tuscan town, which makes Montepulciano d'Abruzzo and, pressed off its skins after a few hours, the cherry coloured rosato Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo. Trebbiano d'Abruzzo is the white, ordinary from most hands and extraordinary from two or three. Pecorino is the rising white. The region holds two DOCGs, Montepulciano d'Abruzzo Colline Teramane and Tullum, and since the 2023 harvest its regional DOCs reserve Superiore and Riserva for named provincial sub-zones such as Terre di Chieti.

terroir.climate: Two climates in one region. The coastal hills are Mediterranean, warm and dry with sea breezes off the Adriatic; the inland valleys and the Peligna basin are continental, with cold winters, late frost and a wide day to night swing. The Apennines, here at their highest, hold back the Tyrrhenian weather, so the growing season is sunny and the autumn long enough to ripen a late grape like Montepulciano fully.
terroir.soils: Calcareous clay is the common ground, heavy on the Chieti plain and lighter in the Teramo hills. River valleys cut down to the sea with gravel and sand on their terraces. The Peligna valley and the high plateau of Ofena around L'Aquila sit on limestone scree and stony clay at altitude, which is where the freshest Montepulciano is grown.
terroir.topography: Mountains take most of the region: the Gran Sasso and the Majella rise close to 3,000 metres within 50 kilometres of the sea. Between them and the coast lie rolling hills, and the vineyards sit there, mostly below 500 metres, with the Peligna basin and the Ofena plateau higher in the interior. The Chieti province alone holds most of the vines.
terroir.water: The Adriatic gives the breezes and the humidity; the Pescara, Sangro, Vomano, Tordino and Tronto rivers run short, steep courses from the mountains to the sea and mark the vineyard valleys.

grapes.name: Montepulciano
grapes.styles: One of the most planted reds of Italy and almost the whole of Abruzzo's red vineyard: deep colour, black cherry and plum, soft tannin and modest acidity; everyday wines by the tanker and long lived ones from a few estates.

grapes.name: Trebbiano Abruzzese
grapes.styles: The true Trebbiano of the region, a distinct vine from Trebbiano Toscano and often confused with Bombino Bianco; neutral at high yields, but from old pergolas and low crops it gives a saline, slowly evolving white that can age for decades.

grapes.name: Trebbiano Toscano
grapes.styles: Permitted in Trebbiano d'Abruzzo alongside the Abruzzese, and the source of much of the plain, crisp wine under that name.

grapes.name: Pecorino
grapes.styles: A mountain white named for the sheep that grazed its vines, rescued from near extinction in the 1980s: early ripening, high in acid and alcohol, with herbs, citrus and a mineral bite.

grapes.name: Passerina
grapes.styles: A simple, fresh white of the Adriatic hills, grown for still, sparkling and passito wines.

grapes.name: Cococciola
grapes.styles: A local white of the Chieti hills with lime and green herb flavours, now bottled on its own.

grapes.name: Sangiovese
grapes.styles: One of the reds allowed to fill up to 15 per cent of Montepulciano d'Abruzzo, and rarely used by the serious estates.

wines.note: Deep purple, black cherry, plum and a touch of earth, with soft tannin and gentle acidity; the most reliable value red in Italy at the everyday end, and a slow, savoury, long lived wine from the Teramo and Pescara hills. Lamb arrosticini, sausages, aubergine and pasta alla chitarra.
The DOCG from the hills around Teramo: fuller structure and firmer tannin than the plain DOC, with a Riserva that spends three years in the cellar. Roast lamb, braised beef, aged pecorino.

A rosato of cherry red depth, far darker than Provence, from Montepulciano left on its skins for hours rather than days: wild strawberry, sour cherry and an almond bitterness, dry and vinous enough for grilled meat and fish stews.

Usually a light, lemony white for seafood; from the rare estates that farm old pergolas and bottle without hurry it becomes waxy, saline and nutty and lives for twenty years. Served cool, not ice cold, with brodetto and fried fish.

Taut and herbal, with lemon, thyme and a stony finish and often fourteen per cent alcohol from its early ripening; sold as Abruzzo DOC or under an IGT. Grilled fish, pecorino cheese and the region's saffron dishes.
The small DOCG around Tollo in the Chieti hills: Montepulciano reds with a Riserva, and Pecorino and Passerina whites under the same name. A local wine worth knowing for its 2019 promotion.

made.viticulture: The sign of Abruzzo is the tendone, the overhead pergola that spreads a canopy at head height over the fruit; it was planted for volume, and the co-operatives of the Chieti plain still crop it heavily for the wine sold by the tanker, but the two most celebrated estates of the region keep theirs on purpose, arguing that the shade protects Montepulciano and Trebbiano from the Adriatic sun and keeps the acidity. Newer plantings are Guyot or spur pruned cordon on the hills. Montepulciano ripens late, into October, and needs the long sunny autumn the mountains guarantee; Pecorino ripens early and is picked in September at full alcohol. Altitude is the lever for freshness: the Peligna valley, Ofena and the Teramo hills give the brightest reds, the coastal plain the softest. Co-operatives founded in the 1960s and 1970s take in most of the region's grapes. The hazards are hail off the mountains, autumn rain at harvest, and a hot summer that flattens the acid of the plain. Organic farming is easy in the dry air and common.
made.winemaking: Montepulciano gives colour and tannin quickly, so most of it is fermented warm for a week or so and bottled young, sometimes after months in large oak or cement, for the soft, fruit led wine the world buys. The slow school is different: long maceration, old large casks or concrete, no fining, late release and bottles that evolve for decades, with one Teramo estate crushing by foot and bottling without filtration. Cerasuolo is Montepulciano pressed off its skins after a short maceration, or run off a red fermentation after a few hours, so it keeps a cherry colour and real tannin; the Riserva reds of the DOC take two years, three for the Colline Teramane DOCG. Trebbiano d'Abruzzo is cool fermented in steel for the quick wine; the rare long lived versions sit on their lees in old wood or cement for a year or more before bottling and are not stabilised cold. Pecorino is made reductively in steel to keep its herbal bite, and some houses give it a few months of lees. Trebbiano is also dried for a small amount of passito.

law.classification: Four regional DOCs carry the names a server meets: Montepulciano d'Abruzzo (1968), Trebbiano d'Abruzzo (1972), Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo (its own DOC since 2010, having been a style of the Montepulciano DOC before) and Abruzzo DOC (2010), which takes the varietal whites such as Pecorino and Passerina. Above them sit two DOCGs: Montepulciano d'Abruzzo Colline Teramane, the Teramo hills, a sub-zone since 1995 and a DOCG since 2003, and Tullum or Terre Tollesi, raised in 2019 around Tollo. A reform in force from the 2023 harvest wrote provincial sub-zones into the regional DOCs, Terre di Chieti, Colline Pescaresi and Terre de L'Aquila, with Colline Teramane added for Trebbiano d'Abruzzo, and reserved the Superiore and Riserva types for wines from those sub-zones with the name printed on the label; a sub-zone Montepulciano asks at least 90 per cent of the grape.
tiers: Montepulciano d'Abruzzo Colline Teramane DOCG
At least 90 per cent Montepulciano from the hills of Teramo province; Riserva three years of ageing with at least one in wood. Sub-zone 1995, DOCG 2003.
Tullum (Terre Tollesi) DOCG
A DOCG of 2019 around the commune of Tollo in Chieti province: Montepulciano reds, Riserva, and Pecorino and Passerina whites.
Montepulciano d'Abruzzo DOC
At least 85 per cent Montepulciano, other local reds to 15; Riserva at least two years of ageing; from the 2023 harvest Superiore and Riserva come from a named sub-zone, at 90 per cent Montepulciano.
Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo DOC
The rosato of Montepulciano, at least 85 per cent, a DOC in its own name since 2010.
Trebbiano d'Abruzzo DOC
Trebbiano Abruzzese and Trebbiano Toscano, at least 85 per cent together; Superiore and Riserva from the sub-zones.
Abruzzo DOC
The regional DOC of 2010 for the varietal whites (Pecorino, Passerina, Cococciola, Montonico), for sparkling wines and for the passito.
Terre di Chieti IGT and Colline Pescaresi IGT
The provincial IGTs under which much of the Pecorino and the Chieti plain's wine is sold.
labels: Cerasuolo
from cerasa, cherry: the deep rosato of Montepulciano, never a red and never a Provence pink
Colline Teramane
the Teramo hills, the DOCG sub-zone of Montepulciano d'Abruzzo
Riserva
two years for Montepulciano d'Abruzzo DOC, three for Colline Teramane
Superiore
higher minimum alcohol; from 2023 reserved for the sub-zones of the regional DOCs
Terre de L'Aquila, Colline Pescaresi, Terre di Chieti
provincial sub-zones printed on Superiore and Riserva labels since the 2023 harvest
Tendone
the overhead pergola of the Abruzzo vineyard
Passito
wine from dried grapes, here mostly Trebbiano or Montepulciano

places.name: Colline Teramane
places.note: The hills of Teramo province in the north, between the Gran Sasso and the sea, the region's first DOCG for Montepulciano and the home of its slowest, longest lived reds; Torano Nuovo and Controguerra are the villages that carry the names of the estates.

places.name: Controguerra
places.note: A village on the Marche border that long carried a small DOC of its own; the Pepe estate's Torano Nuovo lies beside it.

places.name: Colline Pescaresi and Loreto Aprutino
places.note: The hills behind Pescara, where Loreto Aprutino holds the vineyards of Valentini and the region's most famous Trebbiano; a provincial sub-zone of the regional DOCs since 2023.

places.name: Chieti province
places.note: The southern half of the coast and the hills behind it, home to the bulk of the vineyard, the big co-operatives, the Tullum DOCG around Tollo and San Martino sulla Marrucina, Masciarelli's village; Terre di Chieti is its sub-zone name.

places.name: Tollo
places.note: The commune of the Tullum DOCG, raised in 2019 from the Terre Tollesi DOC, for Montepulciano reds and Pecorino and Passerina whites.

places.name: L'Aquila province, the Peligna valley and Ofena
places.note: The high interior west of the Majella: the Peligna basin around Sulmona and the plateau of Ofena under the Gran Sasso, where Montepulciano and Pecorino keep acidity through cold nights; Terre de L'Aquila is the sub-zone name.

places.name: Marche, the neighbour to the north
places.note: The sheet carries no Marche locator, so its wines sit here. Verdicchio is the grape: Verdicchio dei Castelli di Jesi in the hills behind Ancona and the higher, inland Verdicchio di Matelica, with the Riserva of each a DOCG since 2010. Conero DOCG is Montepulciano on the limestone headland above Ancona, Rosso Piceno blends it with Sangiovese, Offida DOCG holds Pecorino and Passerina, and Lacrima di Morro d'Alba is a rose scented red.

places.name: Molise, the neighbour to the south
places.note: A small region between Abruzzo and Puglia with Biferno DOC for Montepulciano and Aglianico reds and Tintilia del Molise DOC for its own native red.

producers.name: Valentini
producers.why: The Loreto Aprutino estate whose Trebbiano d'Abruzzo and Montepulciano, made from old pergolas and sold only in the vintages the house accepts, are the proof that both grapes can be great.

producers.name: Emidio Pepe
producers.why: Torano Nuovo in the Colline Teramane: foot crushed, unfiltered Montepulciano and Trebbiano released after years in the cellar and decanted off their sediment before sale.

producers.name: Masciarelli
producers.why: San Martino sulla Marrucina, founded 1981: the estate that took modern, polished Montepulciano d'Abruzzo abroad, with Villa Gemma as its top bottling.

producers.name: Tiberio
producers.why: A Cugnoli estate in the Pescara hills known for a pure Trebbiano Abruzzese from a single old vineyard and for crisp Pecorino and Cerasuolo.

producers.name: Cataldi Madonna
producers.why: The reference estate of Ofena on the high L'Aquila plateau, known for its Pecorino and for Montepulciano that stays fresh.

producers.name: Illuminati
producers.why: A Controguerra house of 1890 and a founder of the Colline Teramane DOCG, with Zanna as its long aged Montepulciano.

producers.name: Torre dei Beati
producers.why: An organic Loreto Aprutino estate making deep Cerasuolo and single vineyard Montepulciano from the Pescara hills.

producers.name: Praesidium
producers.why: A small Prezza estate in the Peligna valley whose mountain grown Montepulciano shows the freshness of altitude.

producers.name: Cantina Tollo
producers.why: One of the large co-operatives of the Chieti hills, founded 1960, that bottle most of the region's reliable everyday Montepulciano.

exam: Montepulciano is a grape here and a town in Tuscany: Montepulciano d'Abruzzo is the grape, Vino Nobile di Montepulciano is Sangiovese; the most tested Italian trap.
The two DOCGs: Montepulciano d'Abruzzo Colline Teramane (2003) and Tullum or Terre Tollesi (2019). Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo is a DOC of 2010.
Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo is a deep rosato from Montepulciano; cerasa means cherry. Cerasuolo di Vittoria in Sicily is a red blend, a different wine.
Trebbiano d'Abruzzo may be Trebbiano Abruzzese or Trebbiano Toscano; the Abruzzese is the distinct, long lived vine.
Pecorino is a white grape of Abruzzo and Marche named for sheep, not the cheese; Offida DOCG in Marche shares it.
The 2023 reform: provincial sub-zones on the regional DOCs, with Superiore and Riserva reserved for them.
The tendone pergola, the Adriatic, the Gran Sasso and Majella, and the Chieti plain as the volume engine of the region.
Marche across the border: Verdicchio dei Castelli di Jesi and di Matelica, Conero, Rosso Piceno, Offida.
traps: Montepulciano d'Abruzzo is a grape wine; Vino Nobile di Montepulciano is Sangiovese from a Tuscan town. Never let the shared word join them.
Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo is a rosato; Cerasuolo di Vittoria is a Sicilian red DOCG. Same word, two colours.
Trebbiano Abruzzese is not Trebbiano Toscano, though the DOC allows both; neither is Bombino Bianco, despite decades of confusion.
Pecorino the grape and pecorino the cheese share a shepherd, not a flavour.
Colline Teramane is a DOCG inside the Montepulciano d'Abruzzo name; the plain DOC and the DOCG are two tiers of one wine, not two wines.
Abruzzo's Riserva clock is two years for the DOC and three for Colline Teramane; do not carry Brunello's five years here.
The reform of 2023 left the plain DOC at 85 per cent Montepulciano; only the sub-zone wines ask 90.

cards.f: Montepulciano d'Abruzzo DOC: the grape rule
cards.b: At least 85 per cent Montepulciano, other local reds to 15. From the 2023 harvest the Superiore and Riserva come from a named provincial sub-zone and ask 90 per cent.
Montepulciano d'Abruzzo Colline Teramane (Teramo hills, 2003; Riserva three years, one in wood) and Tullum or Terre Tollesi (around Tollo, 2019).
A deep cherry rosato of Montepulciano, at least 85 per cent, from a short skin maceration or a bleed; its own DOC since 2010. Dry, with real tannin; cerasa means cherry.

cards.f: Montepulciano d'Abruzzo or Vino Nobile di Montepulciano: which names the grape?
cards.b: Montepulciano d'Abruzzo: the grape, grown in Abruzzo. Vino Nobile di Montepulciano: Sangiovese from the Tuscan town. No shared grape, no shared place.
The DOC allows Trebbiano Abruzzese and Trebbiano Toscano, 85 per cent together. The Abruzzese is a distinct vine, long confused with Bombino Bianco, and makes the rare long lived whites.
A mountain white of Abruzzo and Marche named for grazing sheep; early ripening, high acid and alcohol, herbal and stony. Sold as Abruzzo DOC, or as Offida DOCG in Marche.
Abruzzo's traditional overhead pergola, planted for volume; most new vines are Guyot or cordon, but the region's two most famous estates keep the tendone for shade and acidity.

cards.f: The 2023 Abruzzo reform in one line
cards.b: The regional DOCs gained provincial sub-zones (Terre di Chieti, Colline Pescaresi, Terre de L'Aquila, and Colline Teramane for Trebbiano), and Superiore and Riserva wines must come from one and print it.

questions.q: Which red grape makes Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo?
questions.exp: Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo is at least 85 per cent Montepulciano, kept on its skins for hours rather than days. Sangiovese leads Tuscany, Aglianico Campania, and Nero d'Avola goes into Sicily's Cerasuolo di Vittoria, a different wine.

questions.q: What colour is Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo?
questions.exp: Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo is a deep cherry rosato of Montepulciano, a DOC of its own since 2010. The red is Montepulciano d'Abruzzo and the white is Trebbiano d'Abruzzo.

questions.q: Which sub-zone of Montepulciano d'Abruzzo holds DOCG status?
questions.exp: The Teramo hills in the north of the region became a sub-zone in 1995 and a DOCG in 2003; the wine asks at least 90 per cent Montepulciano and three years for the Riserva.

questions.q: Which white grape of Abruzzo is named after sheep?
questions.exp: Pecorino takes its name from pecora, sheep, which grazed on its vines in the mountains; it was revived in the 1980s. Passerina, Cococciola and Montonico are other local whites.

questions.q: What is the minimum share of Montepulciano in Montepulciano d'Abruzzo DOC?
questions.exp: The DOC asks 85 per cent Montepulciano with other local reds allowed to 15; the Colline Teramane DOCG and the new sub-zone wines raise the floor to 90 per cent.

questions.q: Which Abruzzo DOCG is centred on the commune of Tollo in Chieti province?
questions.exp: Tullum, also written Terre Tollesi, was raised from DOC to DOCG in 2019 for Montepulciano reds and Pecorino and Passerina whites from the Chieti hills around Tollo.

questions.q: What name does Abruzzo give its traditional overhead vine canopy, spread at head height?
questions.exp: The tendone spreads the canopy overhead at head height; planted for volume, it is kept by the region's most famous estates for the shade and acidity it gives Montepulciano and Trebbiano.

regions.name: Campania
regions.summary: Campania is the region of Naples and Vesuvius, and its serious wine comes from the cold hills of Irpinia inland of the bay, around Avellino. Three DOCGs are the exam's core: Taurasi, the late ripening Aglianico red called the Barolo of the south and the first DOCG granted in the south of Italy, and the two whites, Fiano di Avellino and Greco di Tufo, which age as few southern whites do. A fourth, Aglianico del Taburno, lies in the Sannio. Volcanic ground from Vesuvius and the Campi Flegrei, the Amalfi terraces and Ischia carry the rest. Aglianico del Vulture is the same grape across the border in Basilicata.

terroir.climate: Mediterranean on the bay and the coast, warm and dry, with sea breezes along the Amalfi cliffs and the islands. Irpinia is another country: 400 to 700 metres up in the Apennines, with cold winters, snow, heavy rain and a harvest that runs into November for Aglianico, among the latest of any Italian red. The day to night swing in the hills is what holds acidity in Fiano and Greco.
terroir.soils: Volcanic ground is the region's signature: Vesuvius ash and lava on the bay, the yellow tuff of the Campi Flegrei caldera, the Roccamonfina volcano in the north and layers of pumice and ash that the eruptions spread over Irpinia's clay and limestone. Tufo is named for its tuff and once mined for sulphur; Taurasi's hills are clay and limestone with volcanic layers; the Amalfi coast is limestone and dolomite terraces.
terroir.topography: The Apennines run down the inland spine, and the wine hills of Irpinia and the Sannio sit on their western flank between 300 and 700 metres. The bay of Naples is ringed by Vesuvius to the east and the Campi Flegrei to the west; the Sorrento peninsula and the Amalfi coast drop from 1,000 metre mountains to the sea in terraces, and Ischia and Capri rise offshore.
terroir.water: The Tyrrhenian Sea on three gulfs, Gaeta, Naples and Salerno; the Volturno in the north and the Calore and the Sabato in Irpinia, whose valleys hold the Taurasi and Tufo vineyards. Ischia, Procida and Capri are islands; the Campi Flegrei is a caldera.

grapes.name: Aglianico
grapes.styles: The great red of the south, late ripening, high in acid and hard in tannin, with black cherry, smoke, tar and dried herbs; Taurasi in Irpinia, Taburno in the Sannio, and the Vulture across the border in Basilicata.

grapes.name: Fiano
grapes.styles: Fiano di Avellino: waxy, hazelnut and honeysuckle with pear and smoke, fresh acidity and real weight, and a white that gains honey and toast over a decade; also grown on the coast and in Puglia.

grapes.name: Greco
grapes.styles: Greco di Tufo: taut, stony and high in acid with stone fruit, bitter almond and a flinty edge that growers credit to the sulphur rich ground of Tufo; it ages well but opens sooner than Fiano. A different vine from Calabria's Greco Bianco.

grapes.name: Falanghina
grapes.styles: The fresh white of the Sannio and the Campi Flegrei, two distinct varieties under one name: citrus, green apple and white flowers, unoaked, the region's workhorse white, also made sparkling.

grapes.name: Piedirosso
grapes.styles: Per' e Palummo, dove's foot, for its red stems: the light, peppery red of Vesuvius, the Campi Flegrei and Ischia, soft in tannin and best young.

grapes.name: Coda di Volpe
grapes.styles: Fox's tail, for its long bunch: the white of the Vesuvius slopes in Lacryma Christi Bianco, where the local Caprettone was long confused with it, and a minor partner in Irpinia's whites.

grapes.name: Biancolella
grapes.styles: Ischia's own white, with Forastera, grown on terraces over the sea for lean, saline wines.

grapes.name: Pallagrello
grapes.styles: Pallagrello Bianco and Nero, Bourbon court vines of the Caserta hills revived in the 1990s alongside Casavecchia.

wines.note: Aglianico aged at least three years, one in wood: dark cherry, smoke, tar, leather and dried herbs over high acid and firm tannin, closed when young and best after ten years. Decant; lamb, braised goat, aged caciocavallo.
The same wine held four years with eighteen months in wood, the extra time softening the grip; the Riserva vintages of the old houses can live forty years.
Dry and medium to full, hazelnut, pear, honeysuckle and smoke, with weight more than cut; a white to serve at cellar temperature with roast chicken, mushroom pasta or buffalo mozzarella.

Taut and mineral, peach and quince with bitter almond and a flinty edge from the sulphur ground; higher in acid than Fiano. Oysters, grilled fish and fried seafood; also made as a traditional method sparkling.
Crisp, citrus and apple, unoaked and meant young: the house white of the region's trattorie, with fried anchovies and pizza.
The tears of Christ: a Piedirosso led red from the ash of Vesuvius, light, peppery and sour cherried; the Bianco is Coda di Volpe or Caprettone. Pasta with tomato and the Neapolitan table.
The Sannio's Aglianico DOCG, often softer and earlier drinking than Taurasi, from the hills around Benevento, with two years of ageing and a Riserva at three.
Falanghina and Biancolella from cliff terraces above the sea at Furore: saline, lemon and herb, with a famous barrel fermented Fiorduva from late picked local grapes. Seafood, lemon pasta.

made.viticulture: Irpinia is high, wet and cold for the south, so the choices are those of a mountain vineyard: south and west facing slopes, Guyot and spur pruned cordon replacing the old raggiera and tendone pergolas, and canopy work to dry the fruit after autumn rain. Aglianico buds early and ripens last, picked in late October or November, sometimes after the first snow on the peaks, and its hard tannin needs the full season; it is prone to spring frost and to rot in a wet harvest. Fiano is thick skinned and resists the damp; Greco is tight bunched and rots easily, so growers pick it at the first sign. Phylloxera and the war emptied Irpinia's vineyards, and one Atripalda house kept the three grapes in cultivation, which is why the region still has them. On Vesuvius and in the Campi Flegrei the volcanic sand kept phylloxera out, and ungrafted vines of Piedirosso and Falanghina survive on their own roots. The Amalfi coast and Ischia farm by hand on dry stone terraces over the sea, the Amalfi vines on chestnut pergolas.
made.winemaking: Taurasi is made as a slow red: long maceration to extract and begin softening Aglianico's tannin, then at least a year in wood, in large Slavonian casks by the traditional houses and in barrique by the modern ones, and the balance of its three years in cellar and bottle; the Riserva takes four years with eighteen months of wood. The whites are made in steel, cool and reductive, with a few months on the lees; some Fiano is fermented or aged in used oak for texture, and the best Greco is held on its lees for months before release. Greco di Tufo is also made as a traditional method sparkling wine within the DOCG. Falanghina is fermented cold and bottled early for freshness, and in the Campi Flegrei makes a sparkling base as well. Lacryma Christi reds are fermented briefly for a light, drinkable wine. On the coast, Costa d'Amalfi's top white is barrel fermented from late picked local grapes.

law.classification: Campania holds four DOCGs, three of them in Irpinia: Taurasi, a DOC in 1970 and in 1993 the first DOCG in the south of Italy; Fiano di Avellino and Greco di Tufo, both DOCGs since 2003; and Aglianico del Taburno in the Sannio, promoted in 2011. Irpinia DOC (2005) is the wider umbrella for the province's other wines and its Campi Taurasini sub-zone for younger Aglianico. On the coast and the bay sit the DOCs of Vesuvio with Lacryma Christi, Campi Flegrei, Ischia, Capri, Penisola Sorrentina with Gragnano, and Costa d'Amalfi with its three sub-zones of Furore, Ravello and Tramonti. To the north are Falerno del Massico, Roman Falernian's heir, Galluccio, Aversa for Asprinio and Casavecchia di Pontelatone; the Sannio holds Sannio DOC and Falanghina del Sannio DOC; Cilento covers the south. The IGTs include Campania, Beneventano, Paestum, Colli di Salerno and Terre del Volturno.
tiers: Taurasi DOCG
At least 85 per cent Aglianico from Taurasi and sixteen other communes; three years of ageing with at least one in wood, the Riserva four years with eighteen months in wood. DOC 1970, DOCG 1993.
Fiano di Avellino DOCG
At least 85 per cent Fiano from twenty-six communes around Avellino, Greco, Coda di Volpe or Trebbiano for the rest; the label may add the Latin Apianum. DOCG 2003.
Greco di Tufo DOCG
At least 85 per cent Greco from eight communes around Tufo with Coda di Volpe for the rest; still or traditional method spumante. DOCG 2003.
Aglianico del Taburno DOCG
At least 85 per cent Aglianico from the Taburno massif near Benevento; two years of ageing, three for the Riserva; also a rosato. DOCG 2011.
Irpinia DOC
The provincial DOC of 2005 for varietal Aglianico, Fiano, Greco, Falanghina and Coda di Volpe outside the DOCG rules, with the Campi Taurasini sub-zone for Aglianico.
Vesuvio DOC
Lacryma Christi del Vesuvio: Rosso led by Piedirosso, Bianco by Coda di Volpe or Caprettone, grown on the volcano's slopes.
Costa d'Amalfi DOC
Whites of Falanghina and Biancolella, reds of Piedirosso and Aglianico from the terraces, with Furore, Ravello and Tramonti as named sub-zones.
Falanghina del Sannio DOC
The Benevento province's varietal Falanghina DOC of 2011, with Solopaca, Guardia Sanframondi, Sant'Agata de' Goti and Taburno as sub-zones.
labels: Apianum
the Latin name printed on Fiano di Avellino, from apis, the bee, said to have loved the grape's sweetness
Lacryma Christi
tears of Christ: the Vesuvio DOC's traditional name for its red, white and rosato
Riserva
four years for Taurasi with eighteen months in wood; three for Aglianico del Taburno
Campi Taurasini
the Irpinia DOC sub-zone for Aglianico from the Taurasi communes released young
Furore, Ravello, Tramonti

Per' e Palummo

Spumante

places.name: Irpinia
places.note: The province of Avellino in the Apennines east of Naples, high, cold and wet, where the three DOCGs lie within a few kilometres of each other on clay, limestone and volcanic ash. The first DOCG of the south and the only southern whites with a reputation for ageing come from here.

places.name: Taurasi
places.note: The village on the Calore above Avellino that gives its name to the Aglianico DOCG of seventeen communes; the hills rise from 300 to 700 metres, Montemarano and Castelfranci the highest and latest.

places.name: Montemarano
places.note: The high, cold southern end of the Taurasi zone, above 600 metres, where Aglianico is picked in November and the wines are the most austere.

places.name: Avellino and the Fiano villages
places.note: Fiano di Avellino's twenty-six communes ring the provincial capital, Lapio, Montefredane and Summonte among the names on single vineyard labels.

places.name: Tufo
places.note: A village on the Sabato north of Avellino named for its volcanic tuff, with old sulphur mines under the vineyards that growers credit for the flinty edge of Greco di Tufo; eight communes make up the DOCG.

places.name: Santa Paolina and Montefusco
places.note: Two of the Greco di Tufo communes on the higher ground above Tufo, the source of the most mineral and long lived examples.

places.name: Sannio and the Taburno
places.note: The province of Benevento north of Irpinia, warmer and lower, with the Taburno massif's Aglianico DOCG and the Falanghina del Sannio DOC; Solopaca, Guardia Sanframondi and Sant'Agata de' Goti are its villages and sub-zones.

places.name: Vesuvius
places.note: The volcano east of Naples, whose ash and lava carry the Vesuvio DOC and the Lacryma Christi wines on ungrafted Piedirosso and Caprettone vines; the ancient vineyards at Pompeii have been replanted inside the ruins.

places.name: Campi Flegrei
places.note: The burning fields west of Naples, a caldera of yellow tuff and volcanic sand where Falanghina and Piedirosso grow on their own roots; the DOC names the two grapes as varietal wines.

places.name: The Amalfi coast, Sorrento and the islands
places.note: Costa d'Amalfi DOC on the terraces of Furore, Ravello and Tramonti; Penisola Sorrentina with the fizzy red of Gragnano; Ischia DOC with Biancolella and Forastera; and tiny Capri DOC. All hand worked and saline.

places.name: Caserta and the Massico
places.note: The northern province: Falerno del Massico DOC on Monte Massico and the edge of the Roccamonfina volcano, heir of Rome's Falernian, with Aglianico and Piedirosso reds and Falanghina whites; the Bourbon vines Pallagrello and Casavecchia; Asprinio di Aversa trained up poplars.

places.name: Salerno and the Cilento
places.note: The south of the region: the Cilento DOC on the coast below Paestum, and the Colli di Salerno IGT, under which Montevetrano's Cabernet, Merlot and Aglianico blend opened the south to the world in the 1990s.

places.name: Basilicata, the neighbour to the east
places.note: The sheet carries no Basilicata locator, so its one great wine sits here: Aglianico del Vulture, from the slopes of the extinct Monte Vulture volcano around Rionero and Barile, a DOC since 1971 with Aglianico del Vulture Superiore a DOCG since 2010 (three years of ageing, Riserva five). The same grape as Taurasi, in a different region and on lava rather than clay. Calabria's Cirò, from Gaglioppo, is the other neighbour's red.

producers.name: Mastroberardino
producers.why: The Atripalda house that kept Aglianico, Fiano and Greco alive through the twentieth century and whose Taurasi vintages of the 1960s proved the wine could age; Radici is its Taurasi and it replanted the vineyards of Pompeii.

producers.name: Feudi di San Gregorio
producers.why: Founded in 1986 at Sorbo Serpico, the modern face of Irpinia: polished Taurasi, Fiano and Greco, the Serpico old vine Aglianico and the Pàtrimo Merlot.

producers.name: Quintodecimo
producers.why: A Mirabella Eclano estate founded by a professor of oenology, making single vineyard Taurasi, Fiano and Greco of great polish.

producers.name: Montevetrano
producers.why: A Colli di Salerno IGT blend of Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Aglianico from the hills above Salerno, first made in 1991, that showed the south could make a world class wine outside the DOC rules.

producers.name: Cuomo (Furore)
producers.why: The Amalfi coast estate at Furore sold under its founder's full name, whose Fiorduva, a barrel fermented white from late picked Fenile, Ginestra and Ripoli on cliff terraces, is the coast's one famous wine.

producers.name: Terredora
producers.why: The Irpinia house born of the 1994 division of the Mastroberardino family's vineyards, with Taurasi, Fiano and Greco from its own sites around Montefusco.

producers.name: Pietracupa
producers.why: A small Montefredane estate whose Fiano and Greco are the growers' benchmarks for tension and longevity in Irpinia.

producers.name: Caggiano
producers.why: A Taurasi village estate whose Vigna Macchia dei Goti Taurasi and Salae Domini Aglianico defined the modern, barrique aged style of the 1990s.

producers.name: Molettieri
producers.why: A Montemarano grower at the high, cold end of Taurasi, whose Cinque Querce Riserva is the austere mountain expression of the DOCG.

producers.name: Villa Matilde
producers.why: The Cellole estate that revived Falerno del Massico in the 1960s from the Roman Falernian and makes Aglianico and Falanghina on the Roccamonfina volcano.

producers.name: Mustilli
producers.why: The Sant'Agata de' Goti house that bottled the first varietal Falanghina in 1979 and gave the Sannio its white.

exam: Taurasi: Aglianico at least 85 per cent, three years of ageing with one in wood, Riserva four with eighteen months; DOC 1970, DOCG 1993, the first DOCG in southern Italy.
Fiano di Avellino and Greco di Tufo: both DOCG since 2003, both 85 per cent, both in Irpinia; Fiano waxy and nutty, Greco taut and flinty; Apianum on a Fiano label.
Aglianico del Taburno is Campania's fourth DOCG (2011), in the Sannio; Aglianico del Vulture is Basilicata, with its Superiore DOCG of 2010.
Lacryma Christi del Vesuvio: Vesuvio DOC, Piedirosso red, Coda di Volpe or Caprettone white, ungrafted vines on ash.
Falanghina as the region's everyday white, Falanghina del Sannio DOC and the Campi Flegrei; Piedirosso as Per' e Palummo.
The geography: Irpinia high and cold inland of Naples, harvest into November; the volcanic soils of Vesuvius, Campi Flegrei and Roccamonfina.
The house that saved the grapes after phylloxera and war, and the 1980s and 1990s estates that modernised the region.
Costa d'Amalfi's three sub-zones, Ischia's Biancolella, and Falerno del Massico as the heir of Roman Falernian.
traps: Taurasi is Aglianico from Campania; Aglianico del Vulture is Basilicata. Same grape, two regions, and the atlas keeps Vulture out of the Campania locator.
Greco di Tufo is not Greco di Bianco: the Calabrian wine is a sweet passito from a different vine.
Fiano di Avellino is the DOCG; Fiano grown elsewhere in Campania or in Puglia is only Fiano.
Lacryma Christi is a style within the Vesuvio DOC, not a grape and not a DOCG.
Falanghina is two distinct varieties, Beneventana and Flegrea, under one name; the exam wants only the name.
Taurasi's Riserva is four years, not five; Brunello's clock is Tuscany's.
Aglianico is pale next to Montepulciano and tannic next to everything; do not read its garnet rim as age.
Coda di Volpe is a grape; Caprettone, the Vesuvius white long sold under that name, is a separate vine.

cards.b: Three years with at least one in wood; the Riserva four years with eighteen months in wood. The wine is at least 85 per cent Aglianico, a DOCG since 1993, the first in the south.
Taurasi (1993), Fiano di Avellino (2003) and Greco di Tufo (2003), all in Irpinia; Aglianico del Taburno (2011) in the Sannio.

cards.f: How do Fiano di Avellino and Greco di Tufo differ?
cards.b: Both Irpinia, both 85 per cent, both DOCG 2003. Fiano: waxy, hazelnut, honeysuckle, weight, long ageing, Apianum on the label. Greco: taut, flinty, higher acid, from the sulphur ground at Tufo, also spumante.

cards.f: How does Taurasi differ from Aglianico del Vulture?
cards.b: Same grape. Taurasi: Campania, Irpinia, clay and limestone with ash, DOCG 1993. Vulture: Basilicata, an extinct volcano, DOC 1971, Superiore DOCG 2010.

cards.f: What is Lacryma Christi del Vesuvio?
cards.b: The Vesuvio DOC's traditional name: Rosso led by Piedirosso, Bianco by Coda di Volpe or Caprettone, grown on volcanic ash where vines still stand on their own roots.
Per' e Palummo, dove's foot, for its red stems: a light, peppery red of Vesuvius, the Campi Flegrei and Ischia, soft and best young.
Campania's everyday white, crisp and unoaked; Falanghina del Sannio DOC (2011) and the Campi Flegrei; two distinct varieties, Beneventana and Flegrea, under one name.

cards.f: Why does Irpinia make whites that age?
cards.b: Altitude of 400 to 700 metres, cold winters, a wide day to night swing and clay over volcanic ash: Fiano and Greco keep acid and structure that the coast cannot.

cards.f: Which house kept Irpinia's grapes alive after phylloxera and the war?
cards.b: Mastroberardino of Atripalda kept Aglianico, Fiano and Greco in cultivation after phylloxera and the war, and its Taurasi vintages of the 1960s proved the wine's ageing.

questions.q: Which grape variety makes Taurasi?
questions.exp: Taurasi is at least 85 per cent Aglianico from the hills of Irpinia. Piedirosso makes the light reds of Vesuvius, Montepulciano belongs to Abruzzo and Nero d'Avola to Sicily.

questions.q: Which was the first DOCG granted in southern Italy, in 1993?
questions.exp: Taurasi, a DOC since 1970, became a DOCG in 1993, the first in the south of Italy; Fiano di Avellino and Greco di Tufo followed in 2003.

questions.q: What is the minimum ageing for Taurasi before release?
opts: Four years, eighteen months in wood
questions.exp: Taurasi asks three years with at least one in wood; the Riserva takes four years with eighteen months in wood. Five years and two in wood is Brunello's rule.

questions.q: Which grape must make at least 85 per cent of the DOCG white named for the village of Tufo?
questions.exp: The DOCG is Greco di Tufo: at least 85 per cent Greco from eight communes around Tufo, with Coda di Volpe allowed for the rest. Fiano leads the Avellino DOCG and Falanghina the Sannio's whites.

questions.q: In which region is Aglianico del Vulture made?
questions.exp: Aglianico del Vulture grows on the extinct Monte Vulture volcano in Basilicata, east of Campania. It is the same grape as Taurasi but not a Campanian wine; Puglia lies further east and Calabria to the south.

questions.q: Which grape leads the red Lacryma Christi del Vesuvio?
questions.exp: The Vesuvio DOC's red is led by Piedirosso, the dove's foot grape of the bay, with Sciascinoso and Aglianico as partners; the Bianco is Coda di Volpe or Caprettone.

questions.q: Which white grape gives the crisp, unoaked everyday white of the Sannio and the Campi Flegrei?
questions.exp: Falanghina, two distinct varieties under one name, Beneventana and Flegrea, makes the citrus white of Falanghina del Sannio DOC and the Campi Flegrei. Fiano and Greco are the Irpinian DOCG whites.

questions.q: Which Aglianico wine is the DOCG of the Sannio, near Benevento?
questions.exp: Aglianico del Taburno, a DOCG since 2011, grows on the Taburno massif in the Sannio. Taurasi is Irpinia's DOCG, Aglianico del Vulture is Basilicata's, and Falerno del Massico is a DOC of the Caserta hills.

regions.name: Puglia
regions.summary: Puglia is the heel of Italy, long, flat, hot and dry, with two seas and more vineyard than almost any other region; for a century it sent blending wine north by the tanker, and it still makes more than it bottles. Two red grapes carry the exam: Primitivo, which DNA proved to be Zinfandel, concentrated in Manduria and Gioia del Colle, and Negroamaro, the grape of the Salento and of Salice Salentino. Nero di Troia rules the north around Castel del Monte, which holds three of the region's four DOCGs; the fourth is the sweet Primitivo di Manduria Dolce Naturale. Bush vines, limestone and red clay, and rosato are the region's other signatures.

terroir.climate: Hot, dry Mediterranean, the sunniest and one of the driest regions of Italy, with rain concentrated in winter and summers that run past 35 degrees. The saving graces are wind and water: breezes from the Adriatic on one side and the Ionian on the other cross the narrow Salento, and the Murge plateau's modest altitude cools the nights at Gioia del Colle and Castel del Monte. Drought is the hazard; irrigation is now allowed and used.
terroir.soils: Limestone underlies the whole region, and over it lies terra rossa, the iron rich red clay that colours the Salento and the Murge; sand along the Ionian coast at Manduria; calcareous tufo and thin stony soils on the Murge; deeper alluvial soils on the Tavoliere plain in the north.
terroir.topography: The flattest region in Italy: the Tavoliere plain of Foggia, the Gargano promontory, the long limestone plateau of the Murge running down the middle at 300 to 500 metres, the Valle d'Itria of trulli houses, and the Salento peninsula, almost at sea level between the Adriatic and the Ionian. Hardly a vineyard rises above 500 metres.
terroir.water: Two seas: the Adriatic on the east and the Ionian in the gulf of Taranto to the west, with the Salento a narrow bridge between them. The Ofanto in the north is the one river of size; the rest of the region drinks from aqueducts, and the vineyards rely on the sea breezes for cool.

grapes.name: Primitivo
grapes.styles: The early ripener, named for it, and the same vine as California's Zinfandel and Croatia's Tribidrag: inky, jammy blackberry and plum, high in alcohol, soft in tannin; Manduria on sand gives the richest wines, Gioia del Colle on the Murge the freshest.

grapes.name: Zinfandel
grapes.styles: The Californian name for Primitivo: the exam wants the identity, proved by DNA in the 1990s, and the Croatian name Crljenak Kaštelanski, now Tribidrag, which is the same vine again under its oldest name, not a parent.

grapes.name: Negroamaro
grapes.styles: The black bitter grape of the Salento: dark, plum and dried fig with a bitter, herbal finish and softer tannin than its colour suggests; the base of Salice Salentino and of the region's famous rosato.

grapes.name: Nero di Troia
grapes.styles: Uva di Troia, the late ripening red of the north around Castel del Monte: firmer tannin and higher acidity than the two southern grapes, with violets and black fruit; two of the three Castel del Monte DOCGs are built on it.

grapes.name: Malvasia Nera
grapes.styles: The aromatic dark partner of Negroamaro in Salice Salentino and the Salento reds, adding perfume and softness.

grapes.name: Bombino Nero
grapes.styles: A pale, thin skinned red of the Murge made into the Castel del Monte Bombino Nero rosato, the only DOCG in Italy given to a rosato alone.

grapes.name: Bombino Bianco
grapes.styles: The neutral, high yielding white of the north, once shipped as base wine and now made as a crisp dry white under Castel del Monte and San Severo.

grapes.name: Verdeca
grapes.styles: The white of the Valle d'Itria, in the light wines of Locorotondo and Martina Franca with Bianco d'Alessano.

grapes.name: Susumaniello
grapes.styles: A once vanishing red of Brindisi, deep in colour and juicy, revived as a varietal wine and in rosato.

grapes.name: Fiano
grapes.styles: Grown in the Salento for aromatic whites; the muscat scented Fiano Minutolo of the Valle d'Itria is a separate variety, Minutolo, despite the name.

wines.note: Deep, ripe and warm, blackberry jam, dried fig, cocoa and sweet spice at fourteen per cent and more, with soft tannin and a plush finish; the Riserva takes two years. Lamb, grilled sausages, aubergine parmigiana, or the cheese course.
The DOCG: Primitivo from late picked or dried bunches fermented to a sweet, strong red of prune and chocolate, poured in a small glass with chocolate or aged cheese.
Primitivo from the Murge plateau at around 300 to 500 metres: fresher, less jammy and more savoury than Manduria, with sour cherry and firmer acidity from the cool nights on limestone.
Negroamaro led with Malvasia Nera: dark plum, dried herbs, a bitter chocolate edge and soft grip, the Riserva after two years. Orecchiette with turnip tops and sausage, lamb and roasted peppers.

Negroamaro bled off its skins after a night's contact, deep coral and dry with cherry and bitter orange; Italy's oldest bottled rosato tradition, from 1943, and the region's best match for its fish and vegetable table.

wines.style: Castel del Monte Nero di Troia Riserva
wines.note: A DOCG of structured, violet scented red from the Murge around the Swabian castle, firmer and longer lived than the Salento reds, with two years of ageing.
A pale, dry rosato DOCG from the Bombino Nero grape, the only DOCG in Italy given to a rosato alone; light cherry and citrus, for the aperitivo and the antipasti.
A light, dry white of Verdeca and Bianco d'Alessano from the Valle d'Itria, neutral and crisp, the trulli country's wine with fresh burrata and raw seafood.

made.viticulture: The old Puglian vineyard is the alberello, the free standing bush vine pruned low to the ground that shades its own fruit and survives drought without irrigation; the oldest Primitivo and Negroamaro of Manduria and the Salento still stand this way, some of them on their own roots in the sand, and the best estates buy or rent them. Most of the plain was replanted in the twentieth century to tendone pergolas for table grapes and volume, and to cordon systems for the co-operatives; irrigation, once banned in the DOCs, is now permitted and necessary in a dry summer. Primitivo lives up to its name and is picked from mid August, often in two passes because the same vine carries a second, later crop; Negroamaro follows in September and Nero di Troia in October. The region's enemies are heat and drought rather than rot, so organic farming is easy, but sunburn and raisining on the vine are real, which is where the sweet Dolce Naturale and the old Primitivo style of over fifteen per cent began. Altitude on the Murge at Gioia del Colle and Castel del Monte gives cooler nights and fresher wines than the Salento can.
made.winemaking: For most of its history Puglia made deep, alcoholic wine to be shipped north in bulk and blended into thinner reds, and much of the region's volume still leaves in tankers or as concentrated must. The bottled wines changed from the 1990s, when northern money arrived and the co-operatives learned to control fermentation temperature in a hot September. Primitivo is fermented warm and quickly, its sugar often leaving a few grams of residual sweetness that the style embraces, and aged in large oak or barrique for the Riserva; the Dolce Naturale is fermented from overripe or dried fruit until the yeast stops in the sugar. Negroamaro is macerated for a week or so and kept away from new wood by the traditional houses so that its bitter edge reads as herb rather than tannin; a Salento rosato is made by bleeding the vat after a night on the skins, a method the region has bottled since 1943. Nero di Troia takes a longer maceration and two years for the DOCG Riserva. Verdeca whites are cool fermented in steel and bottled young. Appassimento of Primitivo and Negroamaro for dry, off dry and sweet reds is a growing local habit.

law.classification: Puglia holds four DOCGs, all granted in 2011: three in the north under the Castel del Monte name, Castel del Monte Nero di Troia Riserva, Castel del Monte Rosso Riserva and Castel del Monte Bombino Nero, the last a rosato; and Primitivo di Manduria Dolce Naturale, the sweet red of the Ionian coast. The dry Primitivo di Manduria is a DOC of 1974, with a Riserva. Salice Salentino, a DOC since 1976, is the Negroamaro appellation of the Salento, alongside Brindisi, Copertino, Squinzano, Leverano, Nardò, Alezio and Lizzano. Gioia del Colle DOC holds the Murge Primitivo; Castel del Monte DOC the wider range below its DOCGs; Locorotondo and Martina Franca the Valle d'Itria whites; San Severo and Cacc'e Mmitte di Lucera the Daunia in the north; Moscato di Trani and Aleatico di Puglia the old sweet wines. The IGTs of Salento, Puglia, Tarantino, Murgia, Valle d'Itria and Daunia carry most of the varietal bottlings.
tiers: Primitivo di Manduria DOCG Dolce Naturale
A sweet red from late harvested or dried Primitivo, at least 16 per cent alcohol in all with real residual sugar; DOCG 2011.
Castel del Monte Nero di Troia Riserva DOCG
At least 90 per cent Nero di Troia from the Murge around the castle; two years of ageing, one in wood. 2011.
Castel del Monte Rosso Riserva DOCG
Nero di Troia led, at least 65 per cent, with Aglianico or Montepulciano; two years of ageing with one in wood. 2011.
Castel del Monte Bombino Nero DOCG
A dry rosato of at least 90 per cent Bombino Nero, the only DOCG in Italy given to a rosato alone. 2011.
Primitivo di Manduria DOC

The broad indications under which most varietal Primitivo, Negroamaro and rosato is sold, Salento covering the three southern provinces.

naturally sweet: the sweet Primitivo di Manduria DOCG, with no fortification
Riserva
two years for Primitivo di Manduria, Salice Salentino and the Castel del Monte DOCGs

places.name: Salento
places.note: The peninsula of the heel between two seas, flat, hot and windy, home of Negroamaro, old alberello vines and the rosato tradition; Lecce, Brindisi and the southern half of Taranto province make it up, and Salento IGT is its label.

places.name: Salice Salentino
places.note: A village north of Lecce and the Negroamaro DOC of 1976 named for it, the Salento's most exported red; Leone de Castris, founded 1665, is its historic house and bottled Italy's first rosato there in 1943.

places.name: Manduria
places.note: A town on the Ionian side of Taranto province whose sandy, iron red soils and old bush vines gave Primitivo its DOC in 1974 and its sweet Dolce Naturale DOCG in 2011.

places.name: Brindisi and Copertino
places.note: Two further Negroamaro DOCs of the Salento, Brindisi on the Adriatic port and Copertino inland near Lecce, both with Riserva reds and rosato.

places.name: Gioia del Colle and the Murge
places.note: The limestone plateau between Bari and Taranto at around 300 to 500 metres, where Primitivo was first named in the late eighteenth century by a priest of Gioia del Colle; its DOC of 1987 gives the freshest Primitivo in Puglia.

places.name: Castel del Monte
places.note: The thirteenth century octagonal castle of Frederick II on the northern Murge near Andria gives its name to a DOC and, since 2011, three DOCGs built on Nero di Troia and the Bombino Nero rosato; Rivera is the house most associated with it.

places.name: Valle d'Itria
places.note: The trulli country around Locorotondo and Martina Franca, the one corner of Puglia known for white wine, light and dry from Verdeca and Bianco d'Alessano, with a sparkling tradition.

places.name: Daunia and the Tavoliere
places.note: The north of the region around Foggia: the flat Tavoliere plain, the Gargano promontory, the San Severo DOC and Cacc'e Mmitte di Lucera, with Nero di Troia, Montepulciano and Bombino Bianco; the Daunia IGT.

producers.name: Fino
producers.why: A Manduria estate sold under its founder's full name, whose Es, from old alberello Primitivo vines, is the region's most sought after red and proved that Manduria could be fine rather than merely big.

producers.name: Rivera
producers.why: The Castel del Monte house of 1950 that championed Nero di Troia with its Il Falcone Riserva and was a leading voice for the DOCGs of 2011.

producers.name: Leone de Castris
producers.why: The Salice Salentino estate founded in 1665 that bottled Italy's first rosato, Five Roses, in 1943 and made Salice Salentino a name abroad.

producers.name: Tormaresca
producers.why: The Antinori family's Puglian estates at Castel del Monte (Bocca di Lupo) and in the Salento (Masseria Maìme), part of the 1990s investment that changed the region.

producers.name: Cantele
producers.why: A Salento family house near Lecce known for reliable Negroamaro, Primitivo and Chardonnay at fair prices.

producers.name: Taurino
producers.why: A Guagnano estate whose Patriglione, a Negroamaro from partly dried grapes, became an early cult red of the Salento.

producers.name: Polvanera
producers.why: A Gioia del Colle estate on the Murge whose numbered Primitivo bottlings show the fresher, higher altitude side of the grape.

producers.name: Felline (Accademia dei Racemi)
producers.why: The Manduria group of the 1990s that championed old bush vine Primitivo and revived forgotten local grapes such as Susumaniello.

producers.name: Cantine San Marzano
producers.why: The large co-operative of the Manduria zone whose Sessantanni old vine Primitivo carried the DOC to export markets.

exam: Primitivo is Zinfandel: the same vine, proved by DNA, and the same again as Croatia's Crljenak Kaštelanski or Tribidrag; Manduria and Gioia del Colle are its homes.
Negroamaro is the grape of the Salento and of Salice Salentino DOC (1976), with Malvasia Nera; the rosato tradition dates from 1943.
The four DOCGs of 2011: Castel del Monte Nero di Troia Riserva, Castel del Monte Rosso Riserva, Castel del Monte Bombino Nero (a rosato) and Primitivo di Manduria Dolce Naturale (sweet).
Dry Primitivo di Manduria is a DOC of 1974, Riserva two years; the DOCG is the sweet wine only.
Nero di Troia, also Uva di Troia, is the structured red of the north; Bombino Bianco and Nero are the north's pale grapes.
Puglia's geography: the flattest region, two seas, the Murge plateau, terra rossa over limestone, alberello bush vines, the tanker trade.
Locorotondo and Martina Franca whites from Verdeca in the Valle d'Itria.
traps: Primitivo di Manduria DOC is dry; the DOCG with the same name is Dolce Naturale, the sweet one. Say which you mean.
Negroamaro means black bitter, or black black by another reading; it is not Aglianico and not Nero d'Avola.
Nero di Troia is a Puglian grape most likely named for the town of Troia near Foggia; Homer's Troy is a legend, not a provenance.
Tribidrag is Primitivo under its oldest Croatian name, not its parent; the older course note was loose. The parent idea belongs to Plavac Mali, Tribidrag's child.
Castel del Monte Bombino Nero is a DOCG for rosato alone, the only one in Italy; do not file it with the reds.
Primitivo ripens first, which is what the name means; it is not a primitive or ancient vine in any special sense.
Salice Salentino is a village and a DOC in the Salento; Salento itself is the peninsula and an IGT.
Puglia makes mostly red and rosato; its white Locorotondo is a Verdeca wine, not a Fiano.

cards.b: Zinfandel in California, the same vine by DNA; Croatia's Crljenak Kaštelanski, now called Tribidrag, is the same vine under its oldest name. Named Primitivo for ripening first.
All 2011: Castel del Monte Nero di Troia Riserva, Castel del Monte Rosso Riserva, Castel del Monte Bombino Nero (rosato) and Primitivo di Manduria Dolce Naturale (sweet).

cards.f: Primitivo di Manduria DOC: the rules
cards.b: At least 85 per cent Primitivo from the Ionian coast of Taranto and Brindisi; DOC 1974; minimum 13.5 per cent, Riserva 14 with two years of ageing and nine months in wood. Dry; the sweet one is the DOCG.
Negroamaro, at least 75 per cent, with Malvasia Nera for perfume and softness; a DOC of 1976 from the Salento north of Lecce, with a Riserva after two years.
Dark plum and dried fig with a bitter, herbal finish and softer tannin than its colour; the Salento's grape, and the base of the region's deep rosato.
Uva di Troia, the late ripening, firmer red of northern Puglia around Castel del Monte and Foggia; violets, black fruit, real tannin; two Castel del Monte DOCGs are built on it.

cards.f: Italy's only DOCG for rosato alone
cards.b: Castel del Monte Bombino Nero, from the pale Bombino Nero grape on the Murge; 2011.
The flattest region in Italy: hot and dry between the Adriatic and the Ionian, terra rossa over limestone, the Murge plateau at 300 to 500 metres and the low Salento peninsula.

questions.q: Which grape is genetically the same vine as Primitivo?
questions.exp: DNA matched Primitivo to California's Zinfandel and both to the Croatian Crljenak Kaštelanski, or Tribidrag. Negroamaro, Nero d'Avola and Montepulciano are unrelated southern reds.

questions.q: Which grape leads Salice Salentino Rosso?
questions.exp: Salice Salentino is Negroamaro at 75 per cent or more with Malvasia Nera. Primitivo belongs to Manduria and Gioia del Colle, Nero di Troia to Castel del Monte, Aglianico to Campania.

questions.q: Which style of wine is the Primitivo di Manduria DOCG?
questions.exp: The DOCG of 2011 is Dolce Naturale, a naturally sweet red from late picked or dried Primitivo; the dry Primitivo di Manduria remains a DOC of 1974.

questions.q: Which Puglian DOCG is a rosato?
accept: Castel del Monte Bombino Nero DOCG
questions.exp: Castel del Monte Bombino Nero, raised in 2011, is the only DOCG in Italy given to a rosato alone, made from at least 90 per cent of the pale Bombino Nero grape on the Murge.

questions.q: Which red grape is the base of the Castel del Monte Riserva DOCGs?
questions.exp: Nero di Troia, also written Uva di Troia, makes Castel del Monte Nero di Troia Riserva on its own and leads the Castel del Monte Rosso Riserva; it is the structured red of northern Puglia.

questions.q: Which Puglian DOC grows Primitivo on the limestone Murge plateau?
questions.exp: Gioia del Colle DOC, of 1987, holds the Primitivo of the Murge at around 300 to 500 metres, fresher than Manduria's. Salice Salentino and Brindisi are Negroamaro DOCs of the Salento; Locorotondo is a Valle d'Itria white.

questions.q: What is the Italian name for the free standing bush vine of the old Manduria and Salento vineyards?
questions.exp: The alberello, the little tree, is pruned low with no trellis so that it shades its own fruit and survives drought; the oldest Primitivo and Negroamaro still stand this way, some ungrafted in the sand.
